newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain labour talks look set to end in deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain labour talks look set to end in deal.

text.p: Spain's employers and unions looked set to strike some form of deal on crucial labour reforms on Wednesday, although some of the thornier issues are likely to be put on the back burner for now.

In a last ditch attempt to clinch a deal before the government moves in and forces an agreement, unions and employers returned to the negotiating table on Wednesday after a marathon session of talks on Tuesday that ended in no pact.

There was a flash of hope for a final accord when unions said on Wednesday employers had softened their rigid stance and abandoned their demand for cheaper dismissal costs -- a key sticking point in the talks so far.
While employers would neither confirm nor deny this, they appeared optimistic that a deal could be reached.
"The efforts that both sides are making to come closer to an accord are impressive and there have been advances," Juan Jimenez Aguilar, a spokesman for employers' association CEOE, told reporters.

Struggling to suppress Europe's highest unemployment rate, the government is keen to secure an agreement aimed at liberalising its highly rigid labour market and preparing the economy for European Monetary Union (EMU).
It has given unions and employers until early March to reach a deal before its steps in and imposes a package of measures.
But as unions have pointed out, the government knows an accord needs to be voluntary to be truly effective.
Unions warned earlier this week that government-imposed reforms would fail and lead to labour disputes.
Previous attempts to impose reforms have had little success and liberalisation measures enforced in 1994 by the previous Socialist administration sparked a 24-hour strike.
The main deadlock in negotiations so far has rested in a disagreement over dismissal costs with employers demanding an expansion of current regulations that would effectively cut severance pay.
Having side-stepped this hurdle, unions said Wednesday's talks would now centre on a new contract designed to stimulate jobs for youths who suffer most from unemployment.
Unions have been demanding more contract stability for youths who are often the victim of "junk contracts".
At present, temporary contracts can be renewed only a few times before workers must be made permanent or fired and in most cases employers opt for dismissal.
In the event of no deal, analysts are sceptical the government will be as radical in its reforms as it is threatening to be.
But if they are not tough enough, analysts fear the government could face a worse scenario after joining EMU with unemployment climbing even higher than the current rate of more than 20 percent.
If, as the government hopes, Spain makes the first wave of EMU in 1999, it will no longer have the recourse of devaluing the peseta to help boost the economy and create jobs, analysts point out.
